new mexico.repose_note: New Mexico has no statute of repose for product liability claims.
new mexico.sol_note: Three years from the injury, but the clock starts when the person knows or reasonably should know they were injured, under N.M. Stat. Ann. § 37-1-8 and Martinez v. Showa Denko.
new mexico.state_note: New Mexico uses pure comparative negligence, so an injured person can still recover even if mostly at fault, with the award reduced by their share of fault.
new mexico.strict_note: New Mexico adopted strict liability for defective products in Stang v. Hertz Corp., so the injured person need not prove the seller was careless, only that the product was defective and caused the harm.

new york.repose_note: New York has no statute of repose for product liability claims.
new york.sol_note: Three years from the date of injury under N.Y. C.P.L.R. § 214(5), except toxic-exposure injuries, which run from discovery under C.P.L.R. § 214-c.
new york.state_note: Because there is no repose period, a claim is not barred by the product's age alone, but the three-year clock from injury is strict.
new york.strict_note: New York adopted strict liability for defective products in Codling v. Paglia, so a manufacturer or seller can be liable without proof of carelessness if the product was defective and caused the injury.

north carolina.repose_note: No product claim may be brought more than 12 years after the product was first purchased for use or consumption, under N.C. Gen. Stat. § 1-46.1.
north carolina.sol_note: Three years from the date of injury under N.C. Gen. Stat. § 1-52(5), with the clock starting at discovery for a latent injury that could not reasonably have been found sooner.
north carolina.state_note: North Carolina still uses contributory negligence, so any fault by the injured person can bar recovery entirely, and disease claims are exempt from the 12-year repose period.
north carolina.strict_note: North Carolina has no strict liability in product cases under N.C. Gen. Stat. § 99B-1.1, so the injured person must prove the manufacturer or seller was negligent or breached a warranty.

north dakota.repose_note: North Dakota has no enforceable product-liability repose period because its 10-year repose statute was held unconstitutional in Dickie v. Farmers Union Oil Co.
north dakota.sol_note: Six years from the injury under N.D. Cent. Code § 28-01-16(5), with the discovery rule applying to latent injuries under BASF Corp. v. Symington.
north dakota.state_note: North Dakota is the state's only civil legal-services program, and a seller who did not make the product is usually shielded once the manufacturer is sued.
north dakota.strict_note: North Dakota allows strict liability for defective products, although a non-manufacturer seller can be dismissed after identifying the manufacturer under N.D. Cent. Code § 28-01.3-04.

ohio.repose_note: No product claim may accrue more than 10 years after the product was delivered to its first purchaser or lessee, under Ohio Rev. Code § 2305.10(C)(1).
ohio.sol_note: Two years after the claim accrues, normally the date of injury, under Ohio Rev. Code § 2305.10(A).
ohio.state_note: The 10-year repose period does not apply if the maker committed fraud about the product's safety or gave a written safety warranty longer than 10 years.
ohio.strict_note: Under the Ohio Product Liability Act, a manufacturer is liable if the product was defective in manufacture, design, warning, or representation, and a manufacturing defect can be proved even though the maker used all possible care under § 2307.74.

oklahoma.repose_note: Oklahoma has no statute of repose for product liability claims.
oklahoma.sol_note: Two years from the date of injury under 12 Okla. Stat. § 95(A)(3), with the clock tolled until the injured person knows or reasonably should know of the injury under Oklahoma's discovery rule.
oklahoma.state_note: Oklahoma has no product repose period, so the product's age alone does not bar a claim, but another state's repose law can still apply if the product was bought or registered there, as in Betts v. Toyota (2026).
oklahoma.strict_note: Oklahoma adopted manufacturers' products liability in Kirkland v. General Motors, so a maker can be liable for a defective product without proof of negligence.

oregon.repose_note: A product claim cannot be brought more than 10 years after the product was first purchased for use or consumption, under Or. Rev. Stat. § 30.905(1).
oregon.sol_note: Two years after the injured person first discovers, or reasonably should discover, the injury under Or. Rev. Stat. § 30.905(2).
oregon.state_note: Oregon's 10-year repose period can be longer if the state where the product was made allows more time, and it does not apply at all if that state has no repose period.
oregon.strict_note: Oregon law makes a seller or lessor strictly liable for a product sold in a defective condition unreasonably dangerous to the user, under Or. Rev. Stat. § 30.920.

pennsylvania.repose_note: Pennsylvania has no statute of repose for product liability claims; the 12-year period in 42 Pa.C.S. § 5536 covers improvements to real property, not products.
pennsylvania.sol_note: Two years from the date of injury under 42 Pa.C.S. § 5524(2), with the clock starting only when the injury is discovered in cases of fraudulent concealment.
pennsylvania.state_note: Pennsylvania places no cap on compensatory damages in product cases, and a seller anywhere in the chain of distribution can be strictly liable.
pennsylvania.strict_note: Pennsylvania follows strict liability for defective products under Tincher v. Omega Flex, using a risk-utility or consumer-expectations test for whether the product was defective.

rhode island.repose_note: Rhode Island has no enforceable product-liability repose period because the 10-year limit in R.I. Gen. Laws § 9-1-13 was held unconstitutional in Kennedy v. Cumberland Engineering Co.
rhode island.sol_note: Three years after the cause of action accrues, normally the date of injury or discovery, under R.I. Gen. Laws § 9-1-14(b).
rhode island.state_note: Rhode Island uses pure comparative negligence, so an injured person's own fault reduces but does not bar recovery.
rhode island.strict_note: Rhode Island adopted strict liability for defective products in Ritter v. Narragansett Electric Co., so a seller can be liable even if it used all reasonable care.

south carolina.repose_note: South Carolina has no general statute of repose for product liability claims; its 8-year repose period in S.C. Code Ann. § 15-3-640 covers improvements to real property only.
south carolina.sol_note: Three years from when the injured person knew or reasonably should have known a claim might exist, under S.C. Code Ann. §§ 15-3-530(5) and 15-3-535.
south carolina.state_note: South Carolina caps punitive damages, generally at the greater of $500,000 or three times compensatory damages, under S.C. Code Ann. § 15-32-530.
south carolina.strict_note: South Carolina's strict liability statute, S.C. Code Ann. § 15-73-10, makes a seller liable for a defective, unreasonably dangerous product even if the seller used all possible care.
